risk_heading: Coastal Erosion, Sea Level Rise, and Impacts to Water Resources
paragraph_text:
Some of our assets, suppliers, and logistics routes are located in coastal regions that may be affected by coastal erosion, storm surge, and longer-term changes in sea levels. These changes can damage infrastructure, disrupt transportation, and alter the characteristics and availability of local water resources. For example, saltwater intrusion can contaminate groundwater and increase the salinity of water used in operations, which may require additional treatment or could constrain water usage during peak periods.

We may incur substantial costs to adapt our facilities, such as elevating equipment, strengthening foundations, or installing additional water treatment systems. Such adaptation projects may also face permitting and design constraints. If we cannot implement these measures in time or at reasonable cost, operations could be impaired, and we may experience higher ongoing expenses.

Additionally, coastal changes can affect the availability and quality of certain natural materials sourced in coastal or near-coastal areas. If supply becomes constrained or requires replacement with alternative inputs, our product costs may increase and our ability to meet customer demand could be negatively affected.

Insurance coverage may not fully address the risks, and recovery timelines after major storm events could be longer than anticipated.

risk_heading: Environmental Permitting and Restoration Obligations for Land Disturbance

In some jurisdictions, regulators may require compensatory mitigation for impacts to wetlands or other sensitive areas, which may involve purchasing credits or conducting off-site restoration. If mitigation efforts are not accepted, are delayed, or are subject to additional scrutiny, project costs and schedule impacts may be magnified.

If we fail to comply with permitting conditions or restoration requirements, we could face fines, orders to suspend work, or obligations to perform additional corrective actions. These costs could be material and could adversely affect our ability to execute capital plans.

In addition, delays caused by permitting challenges could result in lost opportunities, customer dissatisfaction, and higher financing costs due to extended construction timelines.

risk_heading: Risks From Changing Water Quality and Treatment Requirements
paragraph_text:
Our facilities rely on water supplies that may vary in quality due to seasonal changes, upstream discharges, extreme rainfall events, and evolving environmental conditions. Increased turbidity, higher salinity, or elevated contaminants—whether from natural causes or anthropogenic sources—could increase the cost and complexity of water treatment required for our operations. In extreme cases, we may need to reduce water usage, change operating parameters, or suspend certain processes while treatment systems are adjusted.

Regulators may also adopt stricter standards governing discharge quality and monitoring frequency, which could require additional infrastructure and operational changes. If we are unable to obtain necessary permits or if our treatment systems are insufficient for new water quality profiles, we could face compliance risks and operational interruptions. Even where we remain compliant, increased treatment needs could raise operating expenses and impact production throughput.

Water quality variations can also affect our supply chain. Some of our suppliers use water-intensive processes and may pass through cost increases or experience production constraints when water treatment becomes more challenging. These conditions could adversely affect our ability to meet customer delivery commitments.

risk_heading: Potential Impairment of Assets Due to Environmental Conditions at Operating Sites

If environmental changes lead to structural damage, reduced foundation integrity, or increased erosion, we may need to incur unplanned capital expenditures to repair or reinforce assets. Such actions could reduce cash available for other initiatives. In addition, changes to local environmental conditions could cause regulatory agencies to revise requirements for stormwater management, flood resilience, or ecological protections, which could require further upgrades.

Some of these risks may also affect property values or our ability to utilize leased space. If we determine that an asset is impaired due to environmental factors, we could be required to recognize impairment charges.

We cannot predict the extent to which these environmental conditions will affect our facilities, nor can we be certain that mitigation measures will be sufficient or affordable within the required timeframes.

risk_heading: Restricted Access to Water-Dependent Transportation and Port Infrastructure
paragraph_text:
We depend on logistics networks that may be influenced by water-related environmental conditions. Port and inland transport infrastructure can be impacted by changes in water levels, sedimentation, and navigability of waterways. For example, extended drought can lower river flows and reduce vessel draft limits, which may require rerouting, scheduling changes, or smaller shipments. Conversely, periods of heavy rainfall can increase sediment runoff and temporarily impair navigability.

If these conditions prevent us from moving goods on a timely basis, we may experience delays in deliveries, increased freight costs, and reduced customer satisfaction. Water-dependent infrastructure can also be subject to stricter environmental standards aimed at protecting aquatic habitats, which may lead to additional operational restrictions or maintenance requirements.

Our reliance on third-party transportation providers and terminal operators introduces additional uncertainty. Even if we take steps to plan for alternative routes, capacity constraints at other ports or increased costs may limit our ability to offset disruptions.

Any prolonged interruption in logistics could adversely affect our revenues, working capital, and ability to fulfill contractual commitments.

risk_heading: Bans or Limitations on Sourcing From High-Risk Ecosystems

Changes to sourcing eligibility could also increase our exposure to supply concentration risk, because alternative sources may be limited or located in other jurisdictions with different environmental requirements.

Failure to adapt to these sourcing constraints could adversely affect our ability to obtain materials needed to manufacture products and meet customer demand.

risk_heading: Dependence on Sustainable Forestry and Land-Management Practices
paragraph_text:
We use materials and components derived from wood and other forest-related inputs. The availability and quality of these inputs depend on long-term land-management practices, forest health, and climate- and ecosystem-related impacts such as drought, pest outbreaks, and wildfire. When forest conditions deteriorate, harvest yields can decline, supply can become volatile, and prices can increase.

We may also face new requirements intended to promote sustainable forestry, including chain-of-custody documentation and restrictions on sourcing from areas associated with illegal logging or land conversion. These requirements can affect the volume of eligible suppliers and may require additional auditing, traceability systems, and contractual provisions.

If we cannot procure sufficient quantities of sustainably sourced inputs, or if we need to transition to alternative materials at higher cost, our ability to produce products on schedule and maintain profit margins could be adversely affected. Customer expectations for responsible sourcing may also increase the likelihood of contract amendments, reporting obligations, or changes in specifications.

Additionally, certain forests are subject to longer supply cycles. If market conditions tighten, the time required to qualify alternative suppliers could reduce our operational flexibility.

risk_heading: Risk of Inadequate Water-Related Infrastructure Capacity
paragraph_text:

In certain locations, local utilities and service providers may face capacity constraints or infrastructure limitations, especially during peak demand periods or extreme weather. If municipal water systems cannot supply required volumes or if treatment capacity is reduced due to upstream quality issues, we may need to implement alternative operating modes or curtail production.

Even when we possess on-site systems, our ability to operate continuously can be constrained by limited storage capacity or the operational reliability of pumps, filters, and treatment media. If these systems fail or become overwhelmed due to unusual water conditions, we could incur significant downtime and repair costs.

Furthermore, our discharge and water-use permits may include limits or monitoring conditions that become more restrictive over time. A tightening of limits could require additional investments, including upgrades to treatment systems or operational changes that affect efficiency.

Our reliance on water-related infrastructure also creates dependency on third parties, including contractors who may be impacted by local environmental disruptions. Failure to maintain adequate water infrastructure capacity could adversely affect our results of operations.

risk_heading: Potential Supply Disruption From Mining and Extractives With Environmental Constraints
paragraph_text:

Suppliers may be exposed to environmental permitting challenges, limitations on water withdrawals, or habitat-protection requirements that can restrict production. Environmental reviews for mining projects can be lengthy, and changes in regulatory expectations for land reclamation, tailings management, and biodiversity protection can slow development or expansion.

If suppliers face restrictions on extracting, processing, or transporting these inputs, our procurement costs may rise and delivery schedules may be affected. Additionally, if a supplier’s operations are halted due to reclamation deficiencies or failure to meet restoration milestones, we may need to qualify alternative sources, which may require substantial lead times.

In some cases, environmental constraints can result in limited availability of certain grades or forms of minerals. Substitutions may require engineering changes or may not perform to specification, which could affect customer acceptance.

We cannot ensure that suppliers will maintain production levels or comply with evolving environmental requirements, and any supply disruption could adversely affect our business and results of operations.

risk_heading: Risks Associated With Wetland Impacts and Stormwater Management Requirements
paragraph_text:
We may operate and expand facilities near wetlands or other environmentally sensitive areas. Stormwater management and related drainage systems can affect nearby habitats, and regulators increasingly focus on minimizing impacts to wetlands and receiving waters. Requirements may include maintaining certain flow rates, ensuring infiltration and runoff controls, and demonstrating that stormwater discharges do not adversely affect ecological conditions.

If our stormwater infrastructure does not meet new or revised requirements, we may be required to undertake capital improvements, conduct additional studies, or modify operations. Mitigation measures could include constructing enhanced stormwater retention systems or implementing green infrastructure that may be more expensive or slower to deploy than conventional engineering solutions.

Because wetlands and drainage characteristics vary by site, small changes in rainfall intensity, ground conditions, or upstream land use can make compliance more challenging. Periodic failure to meet permit conditions could result in enforcement actions or forced operational restrictions.

Any inability to maintain stormwater and wetland-protection compliance could adversely affect our ability to conduct operations and execute planned projects, which could in turn negatively affect our results of operations.

risk_heading: Long-Term Reserve Uncertainty for Environmental Closures and Asset Retirement Obligations
paragraph_text:
We have liabilities associated with environmental closures and asset retirement obligations at certain sites, including obligations to reclaim land and restore natural habitat after operations cease. The timing and scope of these obligations can change based on evolving environmental laws, permit conditions, and the understanding of site conditions over time.

Estimates for such liabilities require assumptions regarding remediation techniques, regulatory approval pathways, monitoring duration, and the expected future cost of labor and materials. If future regulatory agencies require more extensive reclamation measures, or if the remediation approach becomes more complex due to additional findings during monitoring, the amount of required reserves may increase. Additionally, environmental conditions such as flooding, groundwater shifts, or erosion may affect the feasibility of reclamation plans and could increase costs.

If our reserve assessments are revised upward, it could have a material impact on our financial position. Conversely, if actual remediation is less costly than anticipated, reserves may be released into earnings, but such outcomes cannot be assumed.

While we believe our current reserves are appropriate, we cannot predict the ultimate costs to satisfy these natural capital-related closure and restoration obligations.

These requirements can evolve quickly and may differ across jurisdictions and customer segments.

If our current suppliers are not able to meet new sourcing criteria, we may need to renegotiate supply agreements, requalify alternative suppliers, or modify product designs to accommodate different material properties. Such changes can be costly, time-consuming, and may require additional testing to ensure performance and quality.

In addition, documentation and reporting expectations can increase operational burdens for us and for our suppliers. If data is incomplete or inconsistent, compliance could be delayed or contracts may be subject to termination for cause.

We cannot guarantee that market demand will align with our sourcing transitions, that we will be able to obtain compliant materials on favorable terms, or that such changes would not adversely affect our financial condition and results of operations.

risk_heading: Water Availability and Water Quality Could Adversely Affect Our Operations
paragraph_text:
Our operations depend on adequate supplies of water and on maintaining acceptable water quality for manufacturing, utilities, and certain process steps. Increasing water stress in regions where we operate—driven by drought cycles, shifting precipitation patterns, higher temperatures, and increased competition for water—could limit our access to water or increase the cost and time required to secure alternative sources such as municipal supplies, wells, or purchased water. In addition, changes in local water conditions may increase the concentration of naturally occurring contaminants, which could require enhanced treatment, additional chemicals, more frequent maintenance of treatment equipment, or changes to operating parameters.

We also face risks that wastewater discharge permits or water quality standards could be tightened by regulators. If we are unable to comply with permit limits, or if upgrades are delayed or require significant capital expenditures, we could experience production interruptions, increased operating costs, or exposure to enforcement actions and claims from regulators or third parties. Even if we remain compliant, material disruptions to water availability at our facilities or at key supplier sites could negatively impact our ability to meet customer demand and could adversely affect our results of operations.

risk_heading: Biodiversity and Habitat Impacts From Our Land Use and Supply Chain Activities
paragraph_text:
Our activities may affect local ecosystems through land clearing, facility expansion, raw material extraction, transportation routes, and the siting of logistics infrastructure. In some of the regions where we source materials or operate, habitats may be sensitive and home to protected species, including those regulated under federal and state frameworks and, in certain jurisdictions, international conservation agreements. Increased development pressures, stricter enforcement, and evolving scientific assessments can lead to additional permitting requirements, mitigation obligations, or restrictions on operations.

Changes in land use requirements may require us to implement habitat restoration plans, pay for conservation offsets, limit the timing of work to protect breeding cycles, or adjust our sourcing footprint. These actions may increase costs and delay projects, and in certain cases could result in the denial or revocation of permits. If third-party landowners, local communities, or environmental groups challenge our permits or mitigation plans, we could face litigation, administrative proceedings, or temporary work stoppages.

Any inability to adequately manage biodiversity risks, or unexpected findings from environmental studies, could adversely affect our cost structure, expansion plans, and relationships with regulators and land stakeholders.

risk_heading: Soil Contamination and Remediation Liabilities Could Increase Costs
paragraph_text:
We own or lease properties and rely on third parties that may have historical industrial activity or potential sources of contamination, including spills, releases from storage areas, or legacy disposal practices. Even where we believe our sites are being managed appropriately, investigations required by regulators, customer requests, or due diligence in connection with acquisitions, divestitures, or facility transfers can identify conditions that require additional remediation. Soil and groundwater contamination can persist for years and may require long-term monitoring and treatment.

If contamination is discovered or migrates beyond property boundaries, we could become responsible for remediation costs and for costs associated with studies, engineering controls, and potential interim measures. Remediation efforts may also require us to restrict or suspend certain operations, impacting production schedules. In addition, changes in environmental standards or the identification of new contaminants could expand the scope of required corrective actions.

We maintain reserves for environmental matters where appropriate, but reserves may not be sufficient to cover future liabilities, including those arising from changed conditions, unforeseen site conditions, or evolving regulatory interpretation. Any material increase in remediation costs, delays in cleanup, or restrictions on the use of affected properties could adversely affect our financial condition and operating results.

risk_heading: Dependence on Environmentally Sustainable Raw Material Sourcing
paragraph_text:
A portion of our products depends on natural resources whose availability and quality can be affected by environmental degradation, land use changes, and unsustainable extraction practices. For example, certain fiber and agricultural inputs are sensitive to soil health, water availability, drought conditions, and crop diseases. In addition, sourcing may be impacted by deforestation risks, land conversion, and land disputes, which can affect both supply continuity and our ability to obtain certifications or comply with customer and regulatory expectations.

If we cannot secure raw materials from suppliers that meet agreed sustainability criteria, we may face higher costs, increased lead times, or constraints on product output. Our supplier audits and programmatic controls are designed to identify risks, but they may not detect noncompliance by subcontractors, undocumented changes in sourcing origin, or gaps in traceability. Further, natural events such as severe droughts, flooding, or pests can reduce yields and concentrate supply among fewer suppliers, which can increase price volatility.

Regulators may adopt or expand rules requiring proof of responsible sourcing, which could require additional documentation, supplier engagement, and verification. Failure to meet such requirements could result in product delays, reputational harm, loss of certain customer contracts, or regulatory actions.

These factors could materially adversely affect our operations, costs, and ability to meet demand.

risk_heading: Stormwater and Flooding Risks Could Disrupt Our Facilities and Water Systems
paragraph_text:
Our facilities and certain third-party logistics operations are exposed to stormwater events, river flooding, and heavy precipitation. Changes in the frequency and intensity of storms, as well as local drainage constraints, can increase the risk of flooding that damages equipment, contaminates onsite water systems, and disrupts operations. Even when we take preventive measures such as elevating equipment, improving drainage infrastructure, or maintaining emergency response procedures, flooding may exceed design parameters.

Flooding can also affect our ability to handle raw materials, waste streams, and stored goods in a controlled manner, leading to potential releases that may require remediation. If contaminated stormwater enters publicly owned treatment works or receiving waters, regulatory reporting and investigation requirements may apply. In addition, if flood events impair electrical systems or water treatment capacity, we could be forced to shut down production lines until repairs are completed and operating conditions are validated.

We may not have adequate insurance coverage for all flood-related losses, including business interruption, environmental remediation, or third-party claims. Further, repeated storm events could accelerate deterioration of site infrastructure, increasing the likelihood of costly upgrades.

Any significant disruption to our operations, additional remediation obligations, or increased infrastructure and insurance costs could adversely affect our financial results.

Permitting authorities may require detailed environmental assessments, mitigation of impacts to natural resources, and changes to project footprints.

Failure to secure land or required resource approvals on favorable timelines, as well as any resulting redesign or mitigation costs, could materially adversely affect planned capital expenditures and operating results.

The costs of closure and post-closure monitoring can be difficult to estimate because underlying site conditions may not be fully characterized until later stages, and because remedial standards can evolve. Any unanticipated increase in remediation and monitoring costs, delays in achieving regulatory closure, or the inability to maintain required financial assurances could adversely impact our cash flows and profitability.

risk_heading: Supply Disruptions From Drought and Water Rights Restrictions
paragraph_text:
Certain raw materials we purchase require substantial water use during production, processing, or cultivation. As climate variability increases and local water authorities enforce water-rights limits more strictly, suppliers may face mandatory reductions in withdrawals or moratoriums on certain uses. In drought-prone areas, shortages can result in crop losses, lower yields, and interruptions in availability of inputs we rely on.

Even where water is technically available, the cost of meeting withdrawal requirements can increase due to infrastructure upgrades or the need to purchase water from other users. We may not be able to pass through higher procurement costs quickly enough to avoid margin compression, particularly for contracts that set pricing terms in advance.

We work with suppliers to monitor water-related risks and to encourage adoption of water-efficient practices. However, our influence over how third parties manage their water resources may be limited, and supplier efforts may not be sufficient to mitigate severe shortages. In addition, water-related restrictions at one supplier can affect downstream logistics and create ripple effects across multiple tiers of the supply chain.

If we are unable to source alternative inputs or increase production from unaffected regions at commercially reasonable cost and within required timelines, our ability to meet customer demand could be impaired and our results of operations could be adversely affected.

risk_heading: Evolving Requirements for Responsible Land Use and Certification Could Affect Our Costs
paragraph_text:
Customers, investors, and regulators increasingly expect companies to demonstrate responsible land use practices for certain commodities and materials. We rely on suppliers whose production may be associated with land-use change, including expansion into areas previously used for agriculture, forestry, or natural habitat. Although we seek to source from suppliers that meet our standards, the underlying practices may be difficult to verify across multiple tiers, and traceability systems may vary by supplier.

If required certifications or due-diligence rules expand, we may need to invest in additional auditing, traceability technology, supplier training, and documentation. Certification timelines can also be uncertain; a supplier may lose certification due to reasons outside our control, such as local enforcement actions, land disputes, or remediation findings. In such cases, we may face constraints on purchasing and may need to qualify alternative suppliers, which can take time and require additional capital.

We may also incur costs to address nonconformities identified during audits, including remediation commitments, changes in agricultural or extraction practices, or temporary suspensions of procurement. Any failure to meet evolving expectations could result in reputational harm, loss of business, or regulatory scrutiny.

These risks could materially increase our operating costs and adversely impact our supply continuity.

risk_heading: Potential Impacts of Groundwater Depletion on Our Water Supply Agreements
paragraph_text:
We obtain water from municipal utilities and, in certain locations, through contracted groundwater extraction or access to groundwater-dependent infrastructure. Groundwater levels in some service regions have been declining due to long-term demand and changing recharge rates. If local authorities impose pumping restrictions, require reductions in extraction permits, or require additional mitigation fees, our water costs and operational flexibility could be adversely affected.

Where we rely on groundwater-sourced supplies, prolonged declines can also degrade water quality, such as through increased salinity or other dissolved solids, which may require additional treatment capacity and operating costs. If treatment upgrades are not completed on a timely basis, we may experience water delivery interruptions or increased downtime.

In some jurisdictions, water supply agreements may be renegotiated following regulatory actions or changes in permitted volumes. Price adjustments or changes to allocation methods could occur during term renewals, resulting in higher costs. Additionally, third-party utilities may pass through infrastructure repair costs associated with declining groundwater levels.

Although we seek to manage these risks through water conservation initiatives and by evaluating alternative sources, there can be no assurance that such measures will fully offset limitations. Any significant reduction in available water, increased treatment costs, or changes to supply agreements could adversely affect production and profitability.

risk_heading: Failure to Adequately Manage Wetland and Protected Species Constraints Could Delay Projects
paragraph_text:
Some of our operations and planned projects are located near environmentally sensitive areas, including wetlands, riparian zones, and habitats for species that may be protected under applicable law. Environmental review processes may require us to perform baseline surveys, develop habitat protection plans, and obtain approvals before commencing work. These processes can be time-consuming, and outcomes may depend on the presence of certain species, seasonal timing, and the results of ecological assessments.

If surveys identify protected species within the project footprint or migration corridors, we may be required to adopt additional mitigation measures such as seasonal work restrictions, creation of buffer zones, or restoration activities. Such mitigation can increase project costs and lengthen construction timelines. Delays can also occur if regulators require additional information or if public comments lead to reconsideration of permit conditions.

We may also become subject to ongoing monitoring obligations, including reporting on the effectiveness of mitigation measures. Inadequate mitigation or unexpected ecological impacts could lead to permit noncompliance and potential enforcement actions.

Delays or adverse permit determinations can postpone commercialization of assets, increase capital expenditures, and disrupt service levels, which could adversely affect our financial results.

risk_heading: Reliance on Reclaimed and Secondary Materials Exposes Us to Quality and Supply Variability
paragraph_text:
We increasingly consider reclaimed and secondary materials to reduce dependence on virgin natural resources. However, the availability of such materials may fluctuate due to regional recycling rates, contamination levels in recovered streams, changes in commodity prices, and variations in municipal or industrial collection practices. If secondary materials do not meet our required specifications, we may need to blend with additional inputs or revert to virgin sources, which could increase costs and affect customer-facing commitments.

Contamination in recovered materials can also create downstream impacts, including process inefficiencies or increased scrap rates. While we perform incoming inspections and quality testing, not all contaminants may be detected before use, and some issues may only become apparent during production. If the performance of products depends on material purity, quality deviations could lead to customer returns and additional expenses.

Moreover, regulatory changes may affect what materials can be collected, reclaimed, or transported, including restrictions that influence processing requirements for specific streams. Such changes can limit supply or increase processing costs.

If we cannot secure consistent quality and sufficient quantities of secondary materials, our ability to maintain production volumes and meet contractual specifications could be adversely affected.

risk_heading: Land and Environmental Permitting Risks Could Limit Our Ability to Maintain Permitted Wastewater and Discharge Structures
paragraph_text:
We operate facilities that depend on permitted water-related infrastructure, including discharge and treatment systems, stormwater controls, and return-water structures. These systems are supported by permits that require ongoing compliance and periodic reporting. Environmental conditions at our sites can change over time due to erosion, sedimentation, shifting groundwater levels, or modifications in upstream land use.

If regulators require upgrades to reflect updated standards, we may need to invest in additional treatment capacity, monitoring equipment, or structural changes. Permitting processes can impose new conditions that are difficult to implement quickly, including restrictions on timing or volumes of discharges tied to seasonal ecological considerations. Failure to maintain the integrity of drainage systems could also increase the risk of releases into nearby waterways.

In addition, changes to local land use, such as construction activities near our discharge points, can alter runoff characteristics and create operational challenges for our water treatment systems. If such changes cause permit exceedances, we could face penalties, required remediation plans, or temporary suspension of certain operations.

While we maintain compliance programs and conduct inspections, there can be no assurance that our systems will not experience failures or that permit requirements will not change materially. Any significant noncompliance or required upgrades could increase operating costs, constrain capacity, and adversely affect our results of operations.

risk_heading: Deforestation and Deforestation-Related Disruptions in Our Wood and Fiber Supply
paragraph_text:
We procure wood and fiber-based inputs from suppliers that may source from regions exposed to deforestation pressures. Expansion of agricultural land, illegal harvesting, or the loss of tree cover can reduce the availability of sustainably managed timber and can lead to the imposition of restrictions by governments and international buyers. If sourcing regions face increased enforcement or new restrictions, suppliers may be unable to deliver materials on schedule.

We conduct supplier assessments and require compliance with our standards, including documentation intended to support traceability. However, deforestation risks can be difficult to detect, particularly where supply chains include multiple intermediaries and where recordkeeping is inconsistent. If any material we purchase is later determined to be linked to prohibited activities, we could face contractual disputes, cancellation of orders, or demands from regulators for additional investigations.

Regulatory and customer requirements may also require us to demonstrate that our sourcing protects ecosystems and respects land rights. If we must change suppliers or shift to higher-cost certified inputs, our production costs could increase. Additionally, relocation of sourcing to other regions can introduce new logistics complexity and qualification timelines.

Any inability to maintain reliable access to sustainably produced wood and fiber inputs could negatively impact our operations and financial performance.

risk_heading: Coastal and Marine Environmental Risks Could Affect Our Facilities and Intake Systems
paragraph_text:
Some of our facilities and logistics infrastructure operate near coastal or marine environments. These sites may be exposed to coastal erosion, saltwater intrusion into freshwater sources, and changes to marine ecosystems that affect operational intake systems and cooling water availability. Rising sea levels and more severe storms can damage physical assets, disrupt access roads, and impair the performance of drainage and intake structures.

Saltwater intrusion can degrade the quality of groundwater and surface water, increasing treatment requirements and potentially constraining certain processes that depend on fresh water. Additionally, regulatory agencies may require changes to intake and discharge practices to protect marine life, including seasonal or species-based restrictions, leading to downtime or the need for additional filtration or mitigation systems.

We may be required to conduct additional studies or monitoring under permits, and those requirements can increase costs. While we seek to design facilities to withstand reasonable extreme events, unexpected conditions or cumulative damage over time could exceed our engineering assumptions.

Any reduction in water availability, increased treatment costs, or forced changes to intake and discharge practices could adversely affect our production and operating results.

risk_heading: Ground Disturbance and Subsidence Risks Could Trigger Environmental and Safety Obligations
paragraph_text:
We utilize land for manufacturing, storage, and transportation activities that can involve heavy equipment, excavation, and installation of underground utilities. Over time, ground disturbance can contribute to local subsidence, changes in drainage patterns, and increased risk of soil movement or erosion. In some regions, subsidence may also be driven by geologic conditions or by water extraction by third parties.

If subsidence occurs, it may compromise the integrity of foundations, pipelines, and stormwater systems. Water pathways may change, increasing the likelihood of uncontrolled seepage or the migration of contaminants where legacy releases exist. These conditions could prompt regulators to require additional investigations, groundwater monitoring, and corrective actions.

In addition to environmental obligations, subsidence can create safety hazards that require remediation, structural reinforcement, or temporary shutdown of affected operations. Even where no contamination is identified, the cost to stabilize ground and to restore stormwater flows can be significant.

We do not have full control over subsurface conditions at or near our sites, and third-party activities may worsen risks. Any material increase in investigation, monitoring, or remediation costs, or any prolonged operational disruption could adversely affect our financial results.

risk_heading: Risks Associated With Changes in Fish Populations and Water Ecosystems Affecting Our Water Use
paragraph_text:
Some of our facilities rely on surface water withdrawals or discharge into water bodies where ecological conditions can vary due to seasonal cycles, water temperature changes, and fluctuations in fish populations and other aquatic species. These ecosystems may be affected by multiple factors, including pollution from third parties, invasive species, and habitat disruptions. As regulators refine ecological thresholds for withdrawals and discharges, we may be required to modify operating practices.

In certain periods, environmental conditions may reduce available habitat or increase stress on aquatic life, prompting regulators to impose stricter limits, seasonal restrictions, or additional screening requirements for intakes. Implementing such requirements may require capital investments in fish protection equipment, changes to water flow configurations, or operational adjustments that reduce throughput.

While we maintain environmental monitoring and seek permits designed to accommodate seasonal variance, ecological conditions can change faster than permitting processes. If our permits do not sufficiently account for such variability, we could face permit exceedances or compliance actions. Additionally, if third parties contribute to ecological degradation, our ability to obtain regulatory approvals for continued withdrawals may be affected.

Any significant constraints on our water use, increased compliance costs, or interruptions to production could adversely affect our operations and financial results.

risk_heading: Noncompliance With Land Stewardship Obligations in Connection With Planting and Reclamation
paragraph_text:
In connection with certain operations, including the operation of manufacturing sites with adjacent green spaces or the reclamation of previously disturbed land, we may be subject to land stewardship obligations, including commitments to maintain vegetation, prevent erosion, and ensure proper reclamation outcomes. These obligations may be imposed by permits, landowner agreements, or settlement terms following environmental incidents.

Our ability to meet these obligations can be affected by factors outside our control, such as soil composition, weather patterns, invasive species, and the effectiveness of erosion control systems. For example, periods of heavy rainfall may increase runoff and reduce the effectiveness of temporary stabilization measures. Where reclamation performance is measured by vegetation establishment or soil stability metrics, we may need to implement remedial actions such as reseeding, soil amendments, or additional drainage controls.

If monitoring indicates that reclamation or vegetation outcomes do not meet required targets, we could face regulatory notices, increased remediation costs, or extended monitoring obligations. Additionally, failure to comply with land stewardship requirements could impact our ability to renew permits or expand operations.

Although we maintain environmental management procedures, there is no assurance that outcomes will meet required criteria on a timely basis. Any material adverse development in reclamation performance could increase costs and affect operational timelines.

risk_heading: Uncertainty in Carbon-Adjacent Natural Resource Assessments May Affect Permitting
paragraph_text:
Many environmental permitting and impact assessment processes require consideration of natural resource impacts beyond greenhouse gases, including effects on water resources, soil, and habitat quality. In recent years, agencies have expanded their focus on cumulative environmental impacts and on the interrelationship between land, water, and ecosystems. We may need to conduct additional studies to support project approvals, including hydrological assessments, soil and sediment evaluations, and biodiversity surveys.

Because these assessments involve assumptions, modeling techniques, and interpretation of ecological indicators, there is inherent uncertainty in outcomes. If our studies are challenged or if regulators require more conservative assumptions, we may need to revise project designs or expand mitigation measures. Mitigation may include stormwater controls, restoration activities, or additional monitoring for an extended period.

We also rely on third-party consultants to prepare studies and to support engagement with regulators. If the studies contain inaccuracies, incomplete data, or methodological limitations, regulatory review timelines may extend, and we could be required to resubmit materials. In some cases, permits could be conditioned on implementing mitigation actions within specified deadlines.

Such changes can increase costs and delay construction, and may limit the scope of projects that we can pursue. Any inability to secure or maintain permits and approvals based on natural resource impact assessments could adversely affect our expansion plans and operating results.

risk_heading: Restrictions on Waterway Access and Instream Work Could Affect Our Infrastructure Maintenance
paragraph_text:
Our infrastructure and service operations may involve periodic maintenance activities that require access to waterway-adjacent areas, such as repair of culverts, bridges, or drainage systems that connect our sites to stormwater networks. Permits for instream or near-water work can be conditioned on seasonal windows intended to protect aquatic species and maintain water quality. Regulatory requirements can also limit construction methods and require temporary controls to prevent sediment disturbance.

If regulators tighten seasonal or procedural requirements, or if environmental surveys indicate higher ecological sensitivity than expected, our maintenance schedules could be disrupted. Delayed maintenance can increase the risk that drainage or water conveyance systems underperform during heavy rain events, potentially leading to localized flooding, erosion, or additional downstream sedimentation issues.

We may not always be able to shift work to alternate timeframes without increasing costs, and third-party contractors may face similar constraints that limit availability during permitted periods. In some cases, emergency repairs may be subject to heightened scrutiny, requiring additional documentation or approval.

Any inability to perform required waterway-adjacent maintenance within regulatory timeframes could increase operational risks, lead to regulatory findings, and adversely affect our costs and service reliability.

risk_heading: Water Supply and Pricing Volatility Risk

In multiple regions where we manufacture and support customers, demand for water increasingly competes across agriculture, municipalities, and industry. Long-term drought, seasonal variability, groundwater depletion, and regulatory limits on withdrawals could constrain our ability to operate at historical volumes or increase our costs to secure alternative sources. We may be required to install or expand water treatment and recycling systems, procure water from municipal or third-party providers at higher prices, or reduce production during periods of restrictions. These actions could adversely affect our productivity, operating expense, and delivery schedules.

Water risks are further affected by the quality of available supplies. Contamination from upstream industrial activity or municipal systems could require additional filtration and monitoring and could interrupt production if contamination levels exceed specifications. Any disruption could also impact our customers if we are unable to fulfill orders. We cannot assure you that mitigation efforts will be sufficient to address future water stress conditions or that regulatory or market responses to scarcity will not materially and adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.

risk_heading: Land Contamination and Remediation Obligations

In addition, regulators may require remediation to meet standards that change over time or may determine that conditions warrant more aggressive clean-up than previously anticipated. Such requirements could result in significant expenditures, delay redevelopment of property, and increase operating costs.

We may also be required to set aside financial reserves for remediation. If the extent of contamination is greater than expected, or if regulatory requirements become more stringent, our actual obligations could exceed recorded amounts. These developments could adversely affect our financial condition and results of operations.

risk_heading: Raw-Material Sourcing Disruptions From Soil Degradation and Resource Constraints
paragraph_text:
Certain components of our supply chain depend on agricultural or land-intensive inputs. Soil degradation, erosion, salinization, and other forms of land degradation—potentially exacerbated by climate variability—can reduce yields or impair the quality of raw materials. While we do not operate the land used to produce these inputs, we can be affected by changes in farming practices and local productivity.

Additionally, land use conflicts can arise between farming, conservation areas, water extraction, and development. If authorities restrict access to land or water needed for cultivation, suppliers may be forced to curtail production or shift to alternative regions that may not meet our specification requirements. This can lead to increased costs, limited availability, and potential quality issues if sourcing changes abruptly.

We contractually seek to manage sourcing risks through quality standards, supplier audits, and long-term agreements where feasible. However, we may not be able to mitigate all disruptions, especially if multiple suppliers are affected simultaneously or if remediation efforts for degraded land require long lead times. Any material reduction in availability or increases in input costs could adversely impact our operations, margins, and ability to meet customer demand.

Meeting these requirements could increase project costs and extend schedules.

risk_heading: Groundwater Depletion Risk at Manufacturing and Logistics Sites

Certain manufacturing processes require reliable access to groundwater or other subsurface water sources. In regions where aquifers are under stress, water authorities may reduce permitted extraction volumes, introduce metering and monitoring requirements, or require curtailment during drought. If we exceed permitted thresholds—even inadvertently due to variability in operating conditions—we could be subject to fines or forced to stop using certain sources.

In addition, groundwater levels can change naturally and may be affected by increased competition among users. Lower water availability could increase pumping costs and reduce water pressure and quality, which may necessitate changes in process parameters or additional treatment equipment. Such modifications could disrupt production and increase operating expenses.

Where permitted, we may seek alternative supplies or invest in on-site recirculation and efficiency upgrades. However, alternative sources may not be available at comparable cost or may require additional approvals. If we cannot secure reliable water supplies, we may be unable to meet customer requirements or maintain our planned operating rates. These events could materially and adversely affect our results of operations and financial condition.

If coastal and ecosystem-related conditions worsen, or if regulatory requirements change, we could experience operational interruptions and higher costs that adversely affect our results of operations and financial condition.

Restoration requirements may arise years after a facility is closed, including after additional testing or identification of previously unknown impacts. These obligations can be difficult to estimate and may depend on changing regulatory interpretations, remediation technology requirements, and ecological risk assessments. As a result, our ultimate costs could differ materially from our reserves.

We may also face contractual obligations to third parties, including landlords or indemnified parties, to perform or fund restoration. If restoration costs increase or if new environmental standards are adopted, we could be required to fund additional amounts beyond what we have reserved.

Failure to adequately plan for potential restoration liabilities could adversely affect our ability to invest in growth initiatives and could impact our financial condition and results of operations.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Sourcing of Environmentally Preferable Packaging Materials
paragraph_text:
We have initiatives to increase the use of environmentally preferable packaging materials. However, sourcing certain alternatives can expose us to natural capital risks, including forest resource constraints, water-intensive production, and land-use limitations. As demand increases for recycled and sustainably sourced materials, suppliers may face limited feedstock availability or be unable to secure inputs from regions that meet ecological standards.

In addition, forest-based and fiber-based materials may be affected by changes in forest health, including increased pest prevalence, drought impacts, and wildfire-related damage, which can reduce supply and raise costs. Where packaging materials require certification or chain-of-custody documentation, failure of suppliers to maintain compliance could cause us to switch suppliers, reformulate purchasing specifications, or absorb higher prices.

Our procurement teams attempt to diversify suppliers, maintain multi-year contracts where possible, and monitor environmental and sustainability claims. Nevertheless, the environmental certification landscape is evolving and third-party data may be inconsistent across geographies and time periods.

If we cannot secure sufficient quantities of packaging materials at acceptable cost and quality, we may experience production constraints, increased operating expenses, and delivery delays. These effects could adversely affect our results of operations.

risk_heading: Operational Impact From Declining Wetland Quality Near Facilities

Some of our sites border wetlands or are located within watersheds that include sensitive wetlands. Wetlands can provide water filtration, flood attenuation, and habitat for wildlife. Changes in upstream land use, drainage practices, and wastewater inputs by others may degrade wetland quality over time, affecting water availability and the ecological conditions relevant to our facilities.

While our permit obligations address specific site discharges and management practices, degradation of surrounding wetland systems can still result in changes in water chemistry, turbidity, and stormwater runoff that influence operational needs. For instance, higher turbidity may require increased treatment and monitoring for process water used at certain facilities. In addition, increased regulatory attention to wetland impacts could lead to expanded requirements for monitoring and reporting even if our direct discharge volumes are unchanged.

If wetlands continue to degrade or if regulators determine that additional constraints are necessary, we could incur higher costs for water handling and potentially experience restrictions on certain operational activities. These impacts could increase overhead and reduce our ability to operate efficiently.

We cannot assure you that wetland conditions will remain within acceptable parameters or that mitigation investments will be sufficient to prevent operational disruption.

risk_heading: Increased Compliance Costs for Mine Closure, Reclamation, and Land Restoration
paragraph_text:
If we acquire or operate assets involving extraction or use of natural resources, such activities may be subject to reclamation and closure requirements. Regulators may require us to develop and fund reclamation plans designed to restore land contours, soil productivity, vegetation, and water pathways after operations cease. These obligations can include long-term monitoring and maintenance.

Reclamation standards may change based on evolving science and public expectations, potentially requiring additional work beyond what was contemplated when permits were issued. In addition, closure timelines may be affected by commodity cycles or operational decisions, which can influence the cost and feasibility of reclamation. If we are unable to satisfy reclamation obligations or provide required financial assurance, we could face enforcement actions or restrictions on future operations.

We also consider that communities and governmental entities may scrutinize land restoration outcomes, including erosion control and the suitability of restored habitat. If restoration fails to meet expected ecological targets, regulators may require corrective actions that increase costs.

Any failure to properly plan for reclamation and restoration costs, or any unanticipated increase in the cost or scope of compliance, could adversely affect our results of operations and financial condition.

risk_heading: Climate-Linked but Non-Emission Natural Capital Risks to Facilities
paragraph_text:
Although our environmental risk management includes efforts to address weather-related disruptions, changes in natural resource conditions can affect operations through mechanisms that are not limited to greenhouse gas emissions. For example, extreme heat and changing precipitation patterns can increase demand for process water and reduce available supply in our service areas. In addition, higher river temperatures and altered seasonal flow can impact the ability of nearby utilities to provide industrial water within specification.

Our reliance on regional infrastructure means that interruptions in water supply or quality can occur even when our own equipment is functioning properly. We may be required to curtail operations, adjust production schedules, or invest in additional water treatment capacity. Such measures could require permits and engineering work, and may not be completed quickly.

Natural resource conditions can also influence land stability. Increased runoff and soil moisture variability may elevate the risk of slope failures or undermining at sites built on marginal foundations. If this occurs, remediation and stabilization could be expensive and would likely delay projects and capital expenditures.

We cannot assure you that disruptions related to water and land conditions will not occur or that our mitigation efforts will be sufficient to protect our business from material impacts to operations, costs, or customer service levels.

risk_heading: Water Supply and Water Quality Constraints
paragraph_text:
We rely on a combination of municipal and industrial water sources to operate our manufacturing sites, perform processing activities, and support research and development. Many of our facilities are located in regions that have experienced periodic droughts, tightening of surface-water allocations, or restrictions on withdrawals during dry seasons. In addition, stricter discharge requirements can limit our ability to treat wastewater and reuse process water at historical rates or costs. If drought conditions persist, if regulators curtail withdrawals, or if water quality deteriorates due to upstream contamination or extreme weather events, we may experience production slowdowns, increased operating costs, or the need to incur capital expenditures to install additional treatment capacity, alternative sourcing arrangements, or water-efficiency equipment.

Even where we have contingency plans, supply interruptions or inability to meet permitted water-quality thresholds could lead to enforcement actions, higher fees, or temporary shutdowns. Any of these outcomes could materially and adversely affect our results of operations, financial condition, and ability to meet customer demand.

risk_heading: Biodiversity and Ecosystem Impacts from Sourcing and Operations

Expansion of agricultural production, deforestation, and degradation of wetlands or other habitats in sourcing regions could affect the availability, quality, and cost of materials we use. In some cases, environmental conditions such as changes in soil composition, pollinator populations, or local water regimes may reduce yields or require longer processing times, which can create supply bottlenecks. 

We are also subject to increasing scrutiny from customers and regulators regarding biodiversity protection and responsible land management, including requirements that certain suppliers demonstrate traceability and compliance with land-use and conservation standards. If we are unable to obtain required documentation, if key suppliers are impacted by environmental restrictions, or if adverse ecosystem effects lead to interruptions in procurement or increased regulatory burdens, our operating results could be negatively affected.

To mitigate these risks, we work with suppliers on improved environmental practices and monitor supply continuity, but we cannot guarantee that these efforts will fully prevent disruptions or cost increases.

risk_heading: Land Use, Soil Conditions, and Site Remediation Costs

Over time, historic activities by us or prior owners, spills, leaks, or natural processes could result in contamination in soil or groundwater and necessitate remediation under applicable environmental laws. Even when contamination is localized, regulators may require investigations and long-term monitoring, which could delay expansions or limit permissible use of portions of a site.

Remediation requirements can be costly and uncertain as the scope of contamination, identification of responsible parties, and effectiveness of remediation methods may not be known until investigative studies are completed. Additionally, changes in regulatory standards or cleanup technologies could increase the cost or duration of required remediation activities. If we incur remediation expenses beyond what we currently reserve, or if remediation prevents us from using a site as intended, our financial results and operational flexibility may be adversely impacted.

We maintain policies and controls designed to reduce environmental incidents; however, the occurrence of an environmental condition and the associated remediation obligations are inherently difficult to predict.

If land remediation obligations or compliance requirements are imposed on our suppliers, they may pass through costs or face disruptions that affect our delivery schedules. While we attempt to diversify sourcing and incorporate sustainability criteria, we cannot assure that land degradation will not adversely affect our business.

Such delays and additional mitigation requirements could adversely affect our capital expenditure timing and the ability to expand capacity.

These events can also affect the quality of raw materials and process water, including increasing salinity beyond design tolerances.

In response to recurring extreme weather, infrastructure providers and regulators may revise water management rules, impose new stormwater permitting requirements, or require protective upgrades. These changes could require significant capital expenditures to reinforce structures, raise equipment, or modify intake systems and storage practices.

Moreover, damage to surrounding ecosystems from extreme events can create additional compliance obligations, such as restoration requirements or limitations on certain activities during sensitive seasons for aquatic species. If we are unable to maintain uninterrupted operations or incur unplanned capital costs, our results of operations could be adversely affected.

We have taken measures to improve resilience, but the timing, severity, and frequency of extreme weather events remain difficult to predict.

While we maintain multi-sourcing strategies for certain materials, the risks associated with depletion and environmental constraints remain outside our direct control.

We seek to anticipate permitting risks through environmental studies and ongoing stakeholder engagement; however, changes in regulatory standards are not under our control.

Delays or reduced output could adversely affect our ability to fulfill customer orders and may result in higher operating costs.

While we manage water usage and maintain monitoring systems, future heat and drought conditions could create material adverse impacts to our operations.

risk_heading: Climate-Independent Natural Resource Constraints Could Affect Procurement

We may also confront restrictions on land and water use that are unrelated to our direct operations. Governments and water authorities can reallocate supplies during shortages or introduce new allocations and licensing regimes. If suppliers are required to reduce water use, they may curtail production or shift to alternative crops and materials, some of which may not be compatible with our product requirements.

In addition, biodiversity-related policies may restrict certain extraction methods or require seasonal limitations to avoid impacts on wildlife. Such limitations can increase lead times and reduce capacity.

Although we work with suppliers to encourage sustainable practices and perform quality and origin assessments, we cannot guarantee that these efforts will fully mitigate resource constraints in complex upstream systems. Any sustained procurement disruptions could adversely affect our business.

While we maintain water management practices and contingency plans, the effectiveness of those measures may be limited by the local availability of alternative supplies and the capacity of our treatment systems.

While we evaluate these risks as part of our broader operational resilience efforts, we may not be able to offset the impacts of water scarcity or extreme hydrological events through alternative sources at acceptable cost. Supplier continuity may also be affected if upstream water utilities prioritize other uses. Any disruption to our water-dependent operations could adversely affect our ability to meet demand and maintain customer service levels.

If alternative sources are not available on short notice or do not meet required quality specifications, we may be forced to curtail operations or incur significant costs to maintain production. We also must comply with permits and contractual terms governing the use of alternative water sources, which can change with regulatory updates. While we continuously assess our contingency options, any failure of backup supplies to perform as expected could materially affect our operations and financial results.

risk_heading: Water Scarcity and Supply Disruptions Could Increase Our Costs and Impair Operations
paragraph_text:

Local water availability can be affected by drought, changing precipitation patterns, groundwater depletion, and competing municipal or agricultural demands. In jurisdictions where we operate, regulators may impose restrictions on withdrawals, require enhanced water-efficiency measures, or accelerate the closure or modification of well permits. Even where restrictions are not immediate, periodic drought conditions can reduce the reliability of utility supplies or increase the price of treated water and discharge services. In addition, water used in production may be exposed to contaminants that require higher-cost treatment to meet discharge permits and customer specifications.

If water becomes scarce or more expensive, we may be required to curtail production, invest in additional storage and treatment capacity, or redesign processes. These actions could increase operating expenses, reduce throughput, delay deliveries, and harm customer relationships. Any failure to secure adequate water supplies—whether due to regulatory changes, physical water constraints, infrastructure limitations, or failure of third-party suppliers—could adversely affect our business, results of operations, and financial condition.

risk_heading: We May Incur Costs to Comply With Environmental Remediation Obligations at Former or Current Sites

Even where we did not cause contamination, we may be responsible for investigation and remediation under applicable federal, state, and local laws and under contractual arrangements. Cleanup obligations can include monitoring, excavation, treatment systems, and long-term maintenance.

Remediation requirements may increase due to changes in regulatory standards, updated risk assessments, new contamination findings, or the identification of additional contaminants. The scope and timing of remediation efforts can be uncertain and may depend on site conditions and the effectiveness of remedial technologies. Our estimates of liability may be revised based on newly discovered conditions or regulatory directives.

In addition, remediation activities can require permits and community engagement that may delay operations or constrain land use. If remediation costs exceed current reserves, if counterparties do not satisfy indemnification obligations, or if we are deemed responsible for additional environmental impacts, our results of operations and financial condition could be adversely affected.

risk_heading: Climate-Related Changes to Groundwater Levels Could Disrupt Our Supply Chain

Groundwater levels can fluctuate due to prolonged drought, increased extraction, or changes in recharge rates. Where suppliers draw from aquifers, reduced availability can lead to pumping restrictions, higher extraction costs, or the need to source water from alternative systems.

If one or more key suppliers experience groundwater depletion or regulatory limits on well usage, they may reduce output or require longer lead times to procure water. These disruptions could propagate to us through shortages of intermediate inputs, altered product specifications, or increased prices. We may also be required to adopt different supplier standards to address variability in water availability or water chemistry.

Although we work with suppliers to encourage water-stewardship practices, our contractual leverage may not be sufficient to ensure continuity under rapidly worsening conditions. Additionally, suppliers may face community pressure or litigation related to local water impacts.

A significant disruption in the supply chain due to groundwater changes could adversely affect production schedules, customer service levels, and profitability.

Contractor performance and compliance with site-specific mitigation requirements can affect whether mitigation is accepted and whether work can proceed on schedule.

risk_heading: Water Quality Variability May Require Higher-Cost Treatment and Process Changes
paragraph_text:

Water quality can vary due to upstream land-use changes, seasonal runoff, rainfall intensity, and the presence of naturally occurring substances. For example, changes in turbidity or dissolved solids can affect treatment performance and increase chemical usage and filtration cycles.

When water quality deteriorates beyond our historical experience, we may need to increase monitoring, adjust filtration systems, or implement temporary process changes to protect equipment and product quality. In some cases, treatment and process modifications require engineering work and permits, which can cause interruptions or require additional capital expenditures.

Additionally, where we depend on municipal utilities, quality issues can affect the reliability and cost of water provided to us. If utilities face their own supply constraints, they may prioritize certain customers or reduce service reliability, which can increase our downtime.

Our supplier relationships may also be impacted if water quality changes require suppliers to modify their own processing or discharge practices. Any inability to secure water meeting our quality needs, or any requirement to implement higher-cost treatment and process changes, could adversely affect our operations and financial results.

risk_heading: Regulatory Standards for Soil and Groundwater May Increase Our Compliance Burdens
paragraph_text:
Our operations and prior activities may involve the handling of materials that can migrate to soil or groundwater under certain conditions. While we maintain safeguards and monitoring programs, environmental regulatory standards continue to evolve, and agencies may require more extensive sampling, tighter cleanup thresholds, or broader monitoring of adjacent areas.

If regulators determine that conditions at or near our facilities warrant additional investigation or remediation, we may be required to conduct further studies, install or upgrade monitoring wells, and implement remedial systems. Such actions may be expensive and can take significant time to complete, potentially delaying site redevelopment or increasing holding costs for properties.

Moreover, the outcome of regulatory processes may depend on assumptions used in risk assessments, such as exposure pathways and site-specific hydrogeology. If those assumptions change, our obligations could increase even if our operational practices have not materially changed.

We may also be exposed to joint and several liability depending on the nature of the contamination and the activities of other responsible parties. Although we seek to allocate risk through insurance and contractual arrangements, we cannot guarantee full recovery.

Any increase in compliance obligations related to soil and groundwater could materially affect our operating expenses, capital expenditures, and financial condition.

risk_heading: Reputational and Contractual Risks From Non-Compliant Land Management Practices by Suppliers
paragraph_text:
We depend on third-party suppliers for certain agricultural and forestry-based inputs. Stakeholders increasingly expect suppliers to maintain sustainable land management practices, including protection of wetlands, maintenance of forest cover, and responsible use of water resources. Customer requirements and certain financing arrangements can include representations regarding land-use practices and traceability, as well as the right to audit supplier compliance.

If suppliers do not adhere to land stewardship standards—whether due to inadequate oversight, lack of documentation, or circumstances outside their control—our ability to procure eligible inputs may be limited. Contractual consequences could include removal of suppliers from approved lists, requirement to replace inventory, or termination of certain agreements. In certain circumstances, we may also incur remediation or supplier corrective-action costs to address identified deficiencies.

We may face delays if we need to verify sourcing information, conduct additional due diligence, or qualify replacement inputs that meet our specifications. These risks are amplified in regions where recordkeeping systems are limited or where land tenure and monitoring can be difficult.

If we cannot consistently obtain compliant land-managed inputs, our operating results and relationships with customers and partners could be adversely affected.

risk_heading: Changes in Permitted Water Withdrawal Volumes Could Require Costly Process Redesign
paragraph_text:
Some jurisdictions where we operate regulate the amount of water we may withdraw and the conditions under which we may do so. Permitted volumes can be revisited based on updated hydrologic studies, regional water-balance analyses, and observed impacts on local ecosystems. As a result, our future permitted withdrawal volumes may be lower than current levels or subject to stricter seasonal limitations.

If permitted volumes are reduced, we may need to redesign processes, install additional water-reuse systems, increase storage capacity, or shift production schedules to periods when withdrawals are allowed. These upgrades may require engineering work, permitting, and downtime. Even if the required permits are obtained, the time required for installation and validation could affect our ability to meet customer delivery commitments.

In addition, compliance may require more frequent monitoring and reporting. If our measurement systems are not sufficiently accurate or if we experience operational upsets that lead to deviations from permit conditions, we may incur penalties or be required to implement corrective actions.

Any reduction in permitted water withdrawals, or the inability to implement timely process changes to operate within new limits, could adversely affect our operations, costs, and results of operations.

risk_heading: Erosion and Sedimentation at Our Sites Could Require Ongoing Land Restoration
paragraph_text:
Our facilities are subject to erosion and sedimentation risks due to rainfall patterns, storm runoff, and changes in surrounding land conditions. While we maintain control measures designed to limit soil movement, severe weather events can overwhelm drainage systems and increase sediment loads in nearby areas. These conditions can also degrade operational access roads and storage pads.

If erosion control measures do not perform adequately, we could face regulatory inquiries or be required to implement additional mitigation measures. Remedies may include regrading land, installing supplemental erosion barriers, stabilizing slopes, and undertaking sediment removal or revegetation. Such work may require permits and can disrupt operations.

Further, changes in the timing and intensity of rainfall can increase the frequency of events that trigger corrective actions. In addition, new land use developments in the vicinity of our properties could alter runoff patterns, potentially increasing erosion risks on our sites.

Any substantial increase in erosion-related incidents, costs to implement corrective actions, or inability to restore land to regulatory expectations could adversely affect our operating expenses and the ability to maintain our facilities.

risk_heading: Failure to Maintain Sustainable Forestry Practices Could Disrupt Wood-Based Supply

In parallel, regulators and customers may impose or update requirements relating to sustainable forestry practices, chain-of-custody documentation, and protection of critical habitats.

If suppliers are unable to secure timber that meets documentation and sustainability requirements, we may need to source from alternative suppliers or substitute other materials. These changes can result in higher costs, longer lead times, and potential impacts on product performance if substitutes are not fully equivalent. Additionally, transitions may require qualification efforts and adjustments to manufacturing processes.

We also face risks associated with catastrophic events affecting forests, including loss of inventory before shipment or interruptions in transportation infrastructure. While we maintain supplier qualification processes and contractual terms designed to reduce continuity risk, we cannot guarantee that these measures will be sufficient.

Any material disruption in access to compliant, sustainably harvested forestry inputs could adversely affect our production and financial results.

risk_heading: Misestimation of Environmental Impacts Could Lead to Additional Mitigation Costs

These assessments are based on available data and assumptions at the time they are prepared. However, conditions on the ground may change, including seasonal species presence, groundwater characteristics, and hydrologic response to nearby developments.

If subsequent surveys or regulatory reviews identify impacts that were not anticipated, permitting agencies may require additional mitigation measures beyond those originally contemplated. Mitigation can include habitat restoration, long-term monitoring, changes to construction sequencing, or establishment of additional buffers. These requirements can increase costs and delay construction schedules.

Environmental assessments may also be challenged by stakeholders, which can extend public comment periods or trigger additional review. If such reviews require new studies, we may need to pause or modify project activities.

Although we intend to comply with permit conditions and to update assessments when necessary, there is no assurance that mitigation costs will remain within budgeted amounts. Significant additional mitigation obligations could materially adversely affect our cash flows, capital expenditures, and results of operations.

risk_heading: Water Availability and Quality Risk
paragraph_text:
Our operations, including manufacturing, cooling, and cleaning processes, require access to reliable supplies of water. In certain regions where we operate, local authorities and water providers have signaled increased variability in precipitation, higher temperatures, and longer dry periods that can strain municipal and industrial supplies. In addition, water quality can be adversely affected by upstream discharges, aging infrastructure, or extreme weather events that cause sedimentation and contamination. If water becomes unavailable on commercially reasonable terms, or if the quality of water we receive fails to meet internal and regulatory specifications, we may be required to curtail production, install costly treatment systems, or secure alternative sources, such as trucking or supplemental wells, which may be unavailable during drought restrictions.

These outcomes could increase operating costs, reduce throughput, delay shipments, and require additional capital expenditures. While we maintain water management plans and conduct periodic testing, our mitigation efforts may not fully offset the impact of prolonged drought, regulatory changes to discharge permits, or the loss of supplier capacity in water-stressed areas.

risk_heading: Biodiversity and Habitat Disturbance Risk in Sourcing
